question: Competitive Exclusion Principle
content: Gause's Law states that two species competing for the exact same limited resource cannot coexist indefinitely. The species with even the slightest advantage will dominate, driving the other to extinction or forcing it to adapt to a different niche.
description: Two food delivery startups operate in the same city with the same business model, targeting the same restaurants and same customers. After two years, one has 80% market share and the other is shutting down. What principle explains this?
options: One startup had better marketing
The second startup ran out of funding first
the marginally stronger one drives the other out
The market can only support one food delivery company
answer: the marginally stronger one drives the other out
explanation: Gause's Law predicts exactly this outcome. When two competitors have identical niches (same customer segment, same value proposition, same model), they cannot coexist. One gains a marginal advantage and, through network effects and economies of scale, eventually excludes the other entirely.

question: Niche Construction
content: To survive competition, an entity must find or construct a distinct niche where it can operate without direct competition — altering its target audience, geography, or specialization to avoid head-to-head conflict.
description: A new coffee shop wants to open in a neighborhood with three established cafes. Instead of competing on the same menu and vibe, it opens as a late-night coffee bar with board games and live music. What strategy is this?
options: Market saturation — adding more coffee options in the same area
creating a distinct sub-market (late-night + games + music)
Price competition — undercutting the established cafes
Brand marketing — advertising more aggressively than competitors
answer: creating a distinct sub-market (late-night + games + music)
explanation: Rather than fighting the established cafes on their terms (morning coffee, workspace vibe), the new shop constructed a different niche. This avoids direct competition for the same customers at the same time. In its niche, it has no direct competitor — it owns the space.

question: Do Not Be Better — Be Different
content: Trying to beat an entrenched incumbent by copying their strategy is a guaranteed failure. If you target the same customers with the same value proposition through the same channels, the player with more resources will starve you out.
description: A startup tries to compete with Google by building a better general-purpose search engine. Despite superior technology, it gains less than 1% market share. The founder is confused — 'But we are better!' What did they miss?
options: Their search engine was not actually better than Google's
Google has brand loyalty that makes users unwilling to switch
Google's scale advantages made head-to-head competition unwinnable
Search engines are a natural monopoly that no competitor can ever challenge
answer: Google's scale advantages made head-to-head competition unwinnable
explanation: Gause's Law says the incumbent with marginal advantage (scale, data, brand) will dominate if niches are identical. Being 'better' in the same niche is not enough. The winning move is to find a different niche — privacy-focused search, vertical search, AI-native search — where the incumbent's advantages are neutralized.

question: Niche Width
content: A niche can be narrow (specialized) or broad (generalist). Narrow niches reduce competition but also limit total addressable market. The optimal niche balances enough uniqueness to avoid competition with enough size to sustain the organism.
description: A consultant specializes exclusively in regulatory compliance for Swiss watch manufacturers. She has zero competitors but only five potential clients. What is the trade-off she faces?
options: She chose the wrong niche and should broaden her focus
she must balance exclusivity with viability
Five clients are sufficient because they pay premium prices
Swiss watch manufacturers all need compliance consulting
answer: she must balance exclusivity with viability
explanation: Niches are a trade-off. Too narrow: no competitors, but not enough customers to survive. Too broad: lots of customers, but intense competition. The art is finding the right width — a niche where you are the best fit for a customer set large enough to sustain you.

question: Niche as a Secure Base
content: Once you own a niche exclusively, you can use it as a secure base to expand into adjacent ecosystems. The niche provides shelter from which to launch broader incursions.
description: Amazon started as an online bookstore — a narrow niche. From that secure base, it expanded into electronics, cloud computing, media streaming, and groceries. What strategy does this illustrate?
options: Market saturation — dominate one market before expanding
use an exclusive niche as a secure foundation to systematically
Conglomeration — acquire companies in unrelated industries
First-mover advantage — entering each market before anyone else
answer: use an exclusive niche as a secure foundation to systematically
explanation: Amazon started in a defensible niche (online books) where it could establish clear dominance. From that secure base, it expanded into adjacent niches (media, electronics, cloud), each time leveraging capabilities built in the previous niche. The base provides shelter for expansion.

question: Character Displacement
content: When competing species coexist, they evolve to differentiate their niches over time — a process called character displacement. Competitors that initially overlap become different to reduce direct competition.
description: Two social media platforms initially both target 'people who want to share photos.' Over time, one becomes the platform for polished influencer content and the other for private family sharing. What evolutionary process is occurring?
options: Market segmentation — both platforms identified different user groups
the platforms are differentiating their niches to reduce direct competition and
Platform decay — both platforms are losing their original purpose
Consumer preference shifting — users naturally gravitate to different platforms
answer: the platforms are differentiating their niches to reduce direct competition and
explanation: When competitors initially share a niche, competitive pressure drives them to differentiate. The platforms evolve different identities, feature sets, and user expectations. This character displacement allows them to coexist by serving different sub-niches that overlap less over time.

question: Competitive Advantage Through Uniqueness
content: A sustainable competitive advantage comes not from being better at the same game but from playing a different game entirely where your unique capabilities create exclusive value.
description: Two consultancies compete for Fortune 500 clients. One focuses on general strategy. The other focuses exclusively on helping logistics companies optimize supply chains using AI. The second wins nearly every logistics RFP. Why?
options: The second consultancy has better marketing materials
The second consultancy operates in a different niche (logistics +
Logistics companies prefer smaller consultancies
General strategy consulting is not valuable to logistics companies
answer: The second consultancy operates in a different niche (logistics +
explanation: The second consultancy did not try to be a 'better generalist.' It carved a specific niche where its unique capabilities (logistics + AI expertise) perfectly match customer needs. In that niche, it has no real competition because generalists cannot match the depth. Uniqueness beats superiority.

question: Niche Exit Strategy
content: When a niche becomes overcrowded, the rational response is not to compete harder but to exit and find a new niche where competitive pressure is lower.
description: The mobile gaming market is flooded with thousands of new games every month. A studio that was successful five years ago now struggles to get noticed. What strategy does niche theory suggest?
options: Spend more on user acquisition to outspend competitors
Copy the most popular game's mechanics exactly — it worked for others
perhaps AR games, educational games for adults, or games for a
Lower prices to undercut the competition
answer: perhaps AR games, educational games for adults, or games for a
explanation: When a niche is saturated with competitors, the competitive exclusion principle means most will fail. Competing harder (more marketing spend, copying winners) in the same niche is a losing game. The smart move is to find a new niche where you face less competition and can establish exclusive dominance.
